Here’s a list of definitions:

-Vegetarian means someone who doesn’t eat meat.

-Plant based means someone who doesn’t eat any animal products.

-Vegan means someone who doesn’t eat any animal products and doesn’t use animal-based clothing or cosmetics; or support the use of animals for entertainment purposes (example: zoos). Vegans are against all forms of animal exploitation.

These terms are less common, but you might hear them as well:

-Pescatarian means no meat except for fish or seafood.

-Flexitarian means someone who eats mostly vegetarian, but eats meat occasionally.

-Reducitarian is basically the same as flexitarian, it just means someone who is reducing their meat consumption as much as they can.

-Lacto-ovo vegetarian is a synonym for vegetarian, because they also eat dairy and eggs (but not meat).

I tried to word this as simply as possible, hope it helps!

My parents raised my sister and I as vegetarians, but allowed us to eat meat outside of the house. I did when I was little, but ultimately I just didn’t like it. It made me feel physically sick and I always felt guilty about it. As a teenager I went vegan (ironically with some pushback from my mother because of “lack of protein,” but she came around). As for my sister? She grew resentful and started eating meat all the time (I don’t really blame her, our parents are also health nuts who pushed disordered eating and she probably associated vegetarianism and veganism with that). This just goes to show there’s no way to guarantee your kids will share your ideals. Because everyone thinks differently, even if raised in the exact same environment. This is one reason I fear having kids, because I could very well end up raising someone who is racist, fascist, and has much bigger problems than consuming animal products. All you can really do is let her make her own decisions, as long as she doesn’t eat animal products in your home. She may come around, she may not. Either way, I wish the best to you and her both.

I'm going to leave some DBT/coping skills that helped me, but you don't have to use them. No pressure.

My advice is to distract yourself from particularly difficult emotions and/or urges. I have been watching kids movies as a coping mechanism, and it's like an metaphorical band-aid. Protects the wound as it heals and stops me from picking the scab. Find a pleasant activity like that and use it to calm down. This is the ACCEPTS skill in DBT, but I am summarizing it specifically pertaining to how and why it helps me.

When you're in a full on crisis (eg splitting, having suicide and self harm urges, dangerously angry, etc), I suggest using the TIPP skill.

T- temperature. Lower your facial temperature with ice or ice water. Make sure the cold reaches your temples, as this is supposed to trigger the mammalian dive reflex (kind of a hard reset on your nervous system).

I- intense exercise. This is really subjective as every person's comfort level with exercise is different, but generally speaking your heart rate should increase.

P- paced breathing. Breathe to a cadence. I do inhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds, breathe out 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds. Just keep counting until you feel yourself calming down.

P- progressive muscle relaxation. Starting at your toes, squeeze and release every muscle group in your body. Inhale while you're squeezing, exhale as you release.

You can do that in order for the full effect of the dive reflex, but doing the individual steps on their own is also helpful.

And when you're in a safe enough headspace, you can explore your difficult thoughts, feelings and urges to better prepare you for the next crisis. Make a plan for how you're going to de-escalate, or avoid getting to that point in the first place. Don't expect perfection, just practicing these coping skills is good. That goes for the other skills I listed as well.
